headline: When AIs Fight Each Other, Benchmarks Become Obsolete
lede: A brief, oracular quote-tweet from Noah Smith (@Noahpinion) — titled, with characteristic flair, 'The War of the New Gods' — amplifies an observation by @WestleyDang: that traditional cybersecurity benchmarks will soon be eclipsed by frontier AI systems simply hacking one another. The framing is theatrical, but the underlying point is serious. When the attacker and the defender are both superhuman, the most honest measure of either is the other.
body:
For years, the field has evaluated AI hacking capabilities against static human-designed gauntlets: *Capture the Flag* competitions, curated exploit databases, standardised penetration-testing suites. These benchmarks are useful precisely because they are controlled — the same inputs produce comparable outputs across models. But **they were designed for human hackers**, and their ceilings are therefore human ceilings.

The provocative claim here is that GPT-5.5 (OpenAI's reported cybersecurity-capable model variant) and *Mythos* (an Anthropic model apparently specialised for offensive and defensive security, referenced in the YouTube source as 'Claude Mythos') have already outrun the ability of static tests to discriminate meaningfully between them. If two models can both solve every standard CTF challenge, the only informative trial left is to pit them against each other.

This shift has precedent in other domains. Chess and Go rating systems were eventually superseded — for the purpose of evaluating top engines — by self-play and cross-play among the engines themselves. Human-curated positions became irrelevant to the frontier. The same logic applies in security: a benchmark that neither model can fail tells you nothing about which model would survive a live intrusion.

Smith's title, 'The War of the New Gods,' layers a mythological register onto this technical observation. He has written extensively about AI as a civilisational inflection; the phrase signals that he reads the AI-vs-AI dynamic not as a curiosity but as a structural change — the moment when the relevant competition escapes human-legible evaluation entirely. Whether that reading is warranted or merely dramatic depends on how capable these models actually are in unstructured adversarial settings, which neither accessible source makes clear.

The practical stakes are not abstract. If AI-on-AI conflict becomes the primary signal, security researchers lose a neutral third-party arbiter. Whoever deploys the stronger model determines what 'secure' means in practice. Governance frameworks built around human-readable benchmarks would need to be rebuilt from scratch.

concepts.definition: A cybersecurity competition format in which participants solve structured hacking puzzles — finding hidden strings ('flags') by exploiting intentional vulnerabilities. CTFs are widely used to benchmark hacking skill because the challenges are reproducible and scored. Their limitation is that they are designed by humans and thus reflect human-level difficulty ceilings.

The practice of deploying one AI system to attack another, rather than testing against static challenges or human defenders. Borrowed from military 'red team' exercises (adversarial probing of one's own defenses), it produces evaluations that scale with frontier capability but are harder to interpret or standardise.

A standardised test suite used to measure an AI model's offensive or defensive security capabilities — typically curated exploit datasets, vulnerability-detection corpora, or CTF-style challenge sets. They allow reproducible comparisons across models but may become uninformative once all top models saturate the maximum score.

fact_check: The tweet references 'GPT-5.5' while the YouTube source title mentions 'GPT-5.4 Cyber,' suggesting these may be different model versions or that naming conventions are in flux. The available sources do not confirm the exact capabilities of either model in live adversarial settings; the claim that static benchmarks have already been superseded is an inference, not a documented finding. 'Mythos' is identified as a Claude variant in the YouTube source but no authoritative product announcement was accessible to verify its full scope.
